opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so data imbalance is the obvious part of the story. If a tokenizer like BPE is trained mostly on English, Arabic words won't get merged into nice, long tokens, and you end up spending far more tokens to say the same thing. But I think there's something more structural going on with Arabic specifically, and it comes down to morphology.

Arabic is a root-and-pattern language. Most words are built from a consonantal root, often three consonants, like k-t-b, which has to do with writing. Vowel patterns and affixes are then woven around and between those consonants. So you get *kataba*, "he wrote," *kitāb*, "book," *maktab*, "office," *kātib*, "writer," and so on. The meaningful unit, the root, isn't a contiguous substring. It's interleaved with the pattern.

Subword tokenizers like BPE or unigram LM fundamentally operate on contiguous character sequences. They're good at catching things like prefixes and suffixes, the kind of concatenative morphology you see in English, like "un-" or "-ing." But they have no way to represent a discontinuous root. So even with plenty of Arabic data, the tokenizer can't find the segmentation that matches how the language actually builds meaning. It tends to memorize frequent whole-word forms and then fragment everything else in fairly arbitrary ways.

On top of that, Arabic attaches a lot of clitics directly to words: conjunctions like *wa-*, prepositions like *bi-* or *li-*, the definite article *al-*, and pronoun suffixes. A single orthographic word can carry what would be four or five words in English. That multiplies the number of surface forms, so frequency gets spread across many variants and each one is less likely to earn its own token.

Then there's the script. Short vowels usually aren't written, so the same string can be ambiguous. When diacritics do appear, in religious texts or educational material, they create yet another set of surface forms for the tokenizer to handle inconsistently. And there's dialectal variation and code-switching, sometimes in Arabizi, the Latin-script romanization.

So the inefficiency isn't only "we didn't show it enough Arabic." The tokenization approach itself assumes a concatenative, whitespace-friendly view of language that doesn't match Arabic. That's part of why I find tokenizer-free or byte-level approaches interesting, especially ones where the model learns its own segmentation or compression. If the model learns how to group the input, it at least has a chance to discover structure the hand-designed tokenizer could never express, rather than inheriting a segmentation scheme that was suboptimal for the language from the start.

r001.rationale: It explains that Arabic roots are interleaved with vowel patterns and affixes, so the meaningful root is not a contiguous substring.

r002.rationale: It says subword tokenizers operate on contiguous character sequences and cannot represent discontinuous roots, contrasting frequent adjacent-sequence merging with Arabic morphology.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the data imbalance is the thing everyone points to first, and it's real, but it's not the whole story. Even if you trained a BPE tokenizer on a perfectly balanced corpus, Arabic would still come out with more tokens per word than English, and that's because of the morphology of the language itself.

Arabic is a morphologically rich language. Words are built from roots, usually three consonants, and you get different words by interleaving vowel patterns and adding prefixes and suffixes. So a single orthographic word in Arabic can pack in what English would spread across several words. You can have the conjunction, the preposition, the definite article, the stem, and a possessive pronoun all fused into one string with no spaces between them. BPE works by merging frequent character sequences, so it does fine on the stable pieces, but the combinatorics of all those attachments mean the same root shows up in a huge number of surface forms. Each form is rarer than the English equivalent would be, so the tokenizer never learns them as units and ends up splitting them into lots of small fragments.

The other piece is the non-concatenative part. In English, morphology is mostly affixes glued onto the ends of a stem, which is exactly the kind of contiguous pattern BPE is good at capturing. In Arabic the root and the pattern are interleaved, so the meaningful unit isn't a contiguous substring at all. BPE has no way to represent "these three consonants carry the meaning and the vowels between them carry the grammar." It just sees different strings.

And then there are orthographic factors on top of that. Diacritics are usually omitted, but when they do appear they fragment things further. There's variation in how certain letters get written, like different forms of alef or ta marbuta versus ha, which spreads frequency across variants. And Unicode normalization issues can make the same word look like different byte sequences to a byte-level tokenizer.

So when you put all of that together, you get this systematic inefficiency where an Arabic speaker pays more tokens for the same content, which means higher cost, shorter effective context, and often worse downstream performance, and only part of that is fixable by just adding more Arabic data. The rest is really about the tokenization algorithm not matching the structure of the language, which is a big part of why I'm interested in approaches that move away from a fixed subword vocabulary altogether.

r001.rationale: It says Arabic roots and patterns are interleaved, so the meaningful unit is not a contiguous substring.

r002.rationale: It explains that BPE merges frequent character sequences, while Arabic morphology depends on interleaved root and pattern elements that BPE cannot capture as contiguous units.

astra-6.text:
I think a big part of it is the structure of Arabic itself. Subword tokenization works with contiguous chunks of text, but Arabic has this root-and-pattern morphology, where a root’s consonants combine with patterns of vowels and other sounds to form related words. So the meaningful units don’t necessarily line up with the contiguous pieces that a tokenizer can learn.

Arabic also attaches things like conjunctions, prepositions, and pronouns to words, which creates lots of surface forms. A tokenizer might represent those with several pieces without capturing what they share linguistically. So having more Arabic in the training data can help, but there’s also a mismatch between the tokenizer’s assumptions and how the language builds words.

r001.rationale: It says Arabic’s meaningful root-and-pattern units do not necessarily align with contiguous text pieces, conveying that morphological units can be noncontiguous.

r002.rationale: It contrasts subword tokenization’s contiguous chunks with Arabic’s root-and-pattern morphology and explicitly describes a mismatch between them.

sol-6.1.text:
I think a big part of it is the morphology of Arabic. You can have a lot of information packed into a single word, with prefixes and suffixes attached to it. And then there’s the root-and-pattern system, where the root consonants are interleaved with other sounds to form related words. So the meaningful pieces aren’t necessarily contiguous strings that a subword tokenizer can easily learn and reuse.

Even if you increase the amount of Arabic in the tokenizer’s training data, you still have that mismatch. A tokenizer might split a word into several pieces without capturing the structure that connects it to other words. So representation in the training data matters, but so does how well the tokenization method fits the language.

r001.rationale: It says Arabic’s meaningful pieces are not necessarily contiguous strings within a word.

r002.rationale: It describes a mismatch between Arabic morphology and learning contiguous strings, but does not identify subword tokenization’s merging of frequent adjacent units.
